verification.note: Fresh selected primary answers on historical formation, writing for two audiences, revision of Battle Cry and freedom/contingency. sources.title: James M. McPherson, The Fugitives Who Changed America (2015).
sources.citation: James M. McPherson, The Fugitives Who Changed America, New York Review of Books, 4 June 2015; review of Eric Foner, Gateway to Freedom: The Hidden History of the Underground Railroad (Norton, 2015).

verification.note: Fresh original public review main body read. Exact paragraph anchors retain Foner’s specific argument and Sydney Howard Gay record, Madeline Lewis’s discovery and Louis Napoleon’s assistance. Foner’s complete book and manuscript record unread; review is the primary witness to McPherson’s use.

sources.title: James M. McPherson, Dark Victories (2008).
sources.citation: James M. McPherson, Dark Victories, New York Review of Books, 17 April 2008; joint review of Drew Gilpin Faust, This Republic of Suffering (Knopf, 2008), and Mark S. Schantz, Awaiting the Heavenly Country (Cornell University Press, 2008).

verification.note: Fresh public original review main body read, including its qualified final response. Schantz’s and Faust’s different positions are separated. Specific use of Faust on the Good Death, identification and cemeteries does not imply acceptance of her weighting of the war’s meaning. Both complete books unread. Existing queued Faust dossier owns the criticism key; this dossier adds only the contribution key.

sources.title: James M. McPherson, They Chose Freedom (2008).
sources.citation: James M. McPherson, They Chose Freedom, New York Review of Books, 20 March 2008; review of David W. Blight, A Slave No More (Harcourt, 2007).

verification.note: Fresh public original review body and notes 1–6 read. This is a direct later primary witness to the queued McPherson→Berlin/project criticism, not a fresh reading of the 1992 paper or Berlin’s response. Note 3 credits all five editors of Freedom, series I volume 1 (1985), pages 2–3. Blight’s complete book, documentary volume and reviewed narratives independently unread.

sources.title: James McPherson interviewed by Clayton Butler, American Battlefield Trust.
sources.citation: Clayton Butler, An Interview with Historian James McPherson: The War That Never Goes Away, Civil War Trust / American Battlefield Trust, undated public transcript.

verification.note: Fresh selected primary answers on audience, neo-Confederate narratives, recent social/demographic work, formation, title and Woodward’s supervision read. Internal anticipation of the fiftieth anniversary of the August 1963 March suggests 2013; page date not securely established and eight-years-since-retirement claim does not supply an exact date. Raw filename battlefield2013 is a retrieval label only. Gallagher’s childhood Catton reading is explicitly Gallagher’s, not McPherson’s. Review coverage extension: actual Sternhell/new reading and further-scrutiny answers freshly read, including Jim Martin transcript spelling, Hacker, Faust and Blight; additional dispositions in holds.

sources.title: Bertram Wyatt-Brown, America’s Holy War (1997).
sources.citation: Bertram Wyatt-Brown, America’s Holy War, New York Review of Books, 6 November 1997; review of For Cause and Comrades (Oxford University Press, 1997).

verification.note: Fresh selected original main body on ideology, John A. Lynn’s three motivation categories, regional honor/duty criticism and concluding praise, plus notes 1–7 read. Wyatt-Brown’s explanatory resources are his own; no automatic transmission to McPherson. Named critical exchange held because endpoint absent. Complete reviewed book unread.

sources.title: David S. Reynolds, The Commander of Civil War History (2015).
sources.citation: David S. Reynolds, The Commander of Civil War History, New York Review of Books, 19 November 2015; review of The War That Forged a Nation.

verification.note: Fresh selected main body on Woodward’s editorial assignment, synthesis, contingency, soldiers’ ideology and Wiley/Linderman contrasts read. Reynolds’s named scholarly summary is not fresh reading of the reviewed collection or Wiley/Linderman books. Other anecdotal factual claims not independently verified.

sources.title: James McPherson interviewed by Tom Mackaman, 29 October 2012.

verification.note: Fresh full two-page primary interview read; PDF page 2 right column explicitly credits Arno Mayer’s concept of pre-emptive counterrevolution, originally outside the Civil War application. No Mayer endpoint or work/edition specified; held resource. John Hope Franklin’s book is recalled as contemporary publication, without a stated intellectual transfer. HTML guess returned 404; actual PDF succeeded.
